title: Hurricane Nolo Is Crawling Toward Hawaii — And That's the Problem
summary:
Imagine a storm that moves slower than you walk. That's Hurricane Nolo. Right now it's crawling toward Hawaii at only 5 miles per hour — and that slow speed is exactly what makes it dangerous.

On Friday, people on Hawaii's Big Island were put under a hurricane watch. That means hurricane weather could arrive in 24 to 36 hours. Nolo's winds were already blowing at 105 mph, making it a Category 2 hurricane. Forecasters think it could grow into a Category 4 monster with 140 mph winds.

But here's the twist: Nolo probably won't make landfall. Instead, it will sit near the islands and dump rain. A lot of rain. Some spots could get more than 2 feet — that's taller than a kindergarten kid. Most areas will see 10 to 25 inches.

The National Hurricane Center warned of "life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides." Maui is under a tropical storm watch and could get up to 10 inches of rain.

Hawaii has already had a rough year. Four big disasters have damaged or destroyed about 1,290 homes, and Governor Josh Green says recovery could cost around $1 billion. Now Nolo is on the way. "The time to finish preparations... is now," the hurricane center said.
why_it_matters: Learning how storm warnings work — and why slow storms can be the most dangerous — helps you and your family know when to finish preparations and stay safe at home or at school.

background_read: A hurricane is a giant spinning storm that grows over warm ocean water. It loses strength when it moves over cooler water or over land, which is why storms near islands can behave in surprising ways.

Hawaii is a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean, far from the U.S. mainland, so it is not hit directly by hurricanes very often. A powerful hurricane named Iniki still caused major damage on the island of Kauai back in the 1990s.

The National Hurricane Center (a U.S. government office that tracks storms and warns people) rates hurricanes from Category 1 to Category 5 by how strong their winds are, and Governor Josh Green (the leader of Hawaii's state government) said recovery from this year's earlier disasters could cost around $1 billion.
Article_Structure: WHO: Hurricane Nolo, people on Hawaii's Big Island and Maui, Governor Josh Green, and the National Hurricane Center
WHAT: A slow-moving Category 2 hurricane may grow into a Category 4 monster and dump 10 to 25 inches of rain, with more than 2 feet in some spots
WHERE: Near Hawaii, with a hurricane watch for the Big Island and a tropical storm watch for Maui

WHY: The storm's slow speed means it will sit and pour rain, risking life-threatening flooding and mudslides — and Hawaii is still recovering from four earlier disasters that damaged or destroyed about 1,290 homes

perspectives.description: Forecasters and emergency leaders say the message is simple: finish your preparations now, because the rain and mudslides can be deadly even if the storm never makes landfall.
Many families have already lived through four disasters this year that damaged about 1,290 homes, so another huge storm feels exhausting and scary.
Some people hope Nolo stays out at sea or weakens, since forecasters think it probably will not hit land directly — but they still have to get ready just in case.
